awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: CPS: Medium: ASTrA: Automated Synthesis for Trustworthy Autonomous Utility Services
awd_abstract_narration:
Large-scale systems with societal relevance, such as power generation systems, are increasingly able to leverage new technologies to mitigate their environmental impact, e.g., by harvesting energy from renewable sources. This NSF CPS project aims to investigate methods and computational tools to design a new user-centric paradigm for energy apportionment and distribution and, more broadly, for trustworthy utility services. In this paradigm, distributed networked systems will assist the end users of electricity in scheduling and apportioning their consumption. Further, they will enable local and national utility managers to optimize the use of green energy sources while mitigating the effects of intermittence, promote fairness, equity, and affordability. This project pursues a tractable approach to address the challenges of modeling and designing these large-scale, mixed-autonomy, multi-agent CPSs. The intellectual merits include new scalable methods, algorithms, and tools for the design of distributed decision-making strategies and system architectures that can assist the end users in meeting their goals while guaranteeing compliance with the fairness, reliability, and physical constraints of the design. The broader impacts include enabling the automated design of distributed CPSs that coordinate their decision-making in many applications, from robotic swarms to smart manufacturing and smart cities. The research outcomes will also be used in K-12 and undergraduate STEM outreach efforts.
 
The proposed framework, termed Automated Synthesis for Trustworthy Autonomous Utility Services (ASTrA), addresses the design challenges via a three-pronged approach. It uses population games to model the effect of distributed decision-making infrastructures (DMI) on large populations of strategic agents. DMIs will be realized via dedicated networked hybrid hardware architectures and algorithms we seek to design. ASTrA further introduces a systematic, layered methodology to automate the design, verification, and validation of DMIs from expressive representations of the requirements. Finally, it offers a set of cutting-edge computational tools to facilitate our methodology by enabling efficient reasoning about the interaction between discrete models, e.g., used to describe complex missions or embedded software components, and continuous models used to describe physical processes. The evaluation plan involves experimentation on a real testbed designed for zero-net-energy applications.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The ASTrA (Automatic Synthesis for Trustworthy Autonomous Utility Services) project tackled the design of complex decision-making systems for applications such as utility services in smart cities, smart manufacturing, robotic swarms, and intelligent autonomous systems. The project developed scalable methodologies, algorithms, and computational tools to address the challenges of designing distributed, multi-agent, cyber-physical systems that must coordinate their decision-making while guaranteeing reliability, safety, and compliance with design requirements and physical constraints. For example, a large-scale smart city energy distribution grid must enable local and national managers to optimize energy sources and achieve zero-net energy goals. Simultaneously, the system must mitigate the effects of power intermittence and help end-users achieve their objectives in scheduling energy consumption. To address these challenges, the project delivered key innovations in two primary areas:

Scalable Design Space Exploration and Requirement Validation. The design space exploration of complex system architectures often relies on solving optimization problems whose computational costs become daunting as the system grows. We proposed general formulations of the architecture exploration problem that improve on the scalability of prior work, capture a broader set of design aspects, and allow solving problems that were previously intractable. We also introduced effective solution strategies that combine compositional reasoning via assume-guarantee contracts with efficient methods to prune the search space. A paper in this area received the Best Paper Award from the 2024 Design, Automation, and Test in Europe Conference (DATE).

We leveraged contracts to enable modular and tractable exploration beyond the limitations shown by prior methods. Contracts clearly define what a specific system component expects from its environment (assumptions) and what it promises to deliver in return (guarantees). We expressed contracts using mathematical formulas, specifically following a paradigm called satisfiability modulo convex (SMC) programming, to effectively model the interdependencies between architectural configurations and functional properties. We could then build on the effectiveness of the SMC paradigm in reasoning about combinations of discrete (logical) and continuous (dynamical) constraints and extended it to solve complex optimization problems.

Safe and Optimal Decision-Making and Control Under Uncertainty. We designed decision-making and control algorithms with provable guarantees on the satisfaction of dynamic constraints and specifications expressed by logic languages under uncertainty. In distributed decision-making systems, large populations of learning agents can act non-cooperatively and interact with a dynamical system, potentially driving it into undesirable states and compromising its stability and safety. To mitigate these risks, we proposed a method using control barrier functions (CBFs) to design incentive mechanisms that guide the population's decisions to a desired state while ensuring safe and stable behaviors. We also established general conditions under which the designed incentives remain effective across different classes of learning agents, ensuring broad applicability.

By formulating time-varying CBFs in terms of contracts, we provided an interface bridging high-level task planning and low-level feedback control in the design of autonomous agents subject to time-varying constraints and mission specifications in temporal logic. Our methods ensure that correctness and trustworthiness guarantees established at higher abstraction levels propagate consistently to the implementation level.

We also contributed a theory of optimal decision-making for agents described by Markov decision processes (MDPs) and partially observable MDPs (POMDPs), aiming to optimize a reward objective, for example, communication latency or energy consumption, with provable probabilistic guarantees on the satisfaction of temporal logic specifications. We studied single-agent scenarios as well as multi-agent scenarios, in which a team of agents has a common objective but disparate information structures and temporal logic constraints. In the multi-agent setting, we demonstrated a methodology to decompose the optimal decision-making problem into more manageable pieces, achieving near-optimal policies, while reducing problem size and execution time by an order of magnitude. For single agents interacting with unknown dynamics that must be learned online, we contributed a safe posterior sampling-based reinforcement learning algorithm that guarantees bounded-time violation of safety constraints and outperforms prior approaches.

Broader Impacts. The methodologies developed by the ASTrA team were successfully demonstrated in realistic resource allocation scenarios, particularly in supporting renewable energy utilization and electric vehicle charging grids. Beyond technical achievements, the project had a significant impact on education and community building by fostering collaboration between academia and industry. Results were widely shared through open-source toolkits, workshops, invited seminars, and publications. Most importantly, the project trained a new generation of graduate students and junior researchers in critical fields like artificial intelligence, game theory, control theory, formal methods, and cyber-physical systems. Ultimately, the ASTrA project laid a vital foundation for a future where large populations of learning agents can safely and reliably interact with our most critical infrastructure.
